You use the imperfect subjunctive after como si (as if), ojalá (almost impossible wishes), me gustaría que / preferiría que and aunque (even if, hypothetical).
He speaks Romanian as if he were from here.
If only I spoke perfect Romanian!
I’d like my pupils to speak more.
She looked at me as if she didn’t know me.
Even if I were scared, I wouldn’t say so.
To use como si + imperfect subjunctive (ALWAYS, whatever the tense).
To tell ojalá + present subj. (possible wish) from ojalá + imperfect subj. (unlikely wish).
To express polite wishes: me gustaría que / preferiría que + imperfect subj.
To use aunque with the indicative (fact) and with the subjunctive (hypothesis).
To describe your first day somewhere new.
March, Bucharest. Ana is starting to teach Spanish at a bilingual secondary school. The head teacher, Mrs Popescu, speaks Spanish. She greets her at the door.
Welcome, Ana. Come in, come in. Make yourself at home.
Thank you very much, Mrs Popescu. You speak Spanish as if you were Spanish.
I lived in Valencia for five years when I was young. If only I could go back more often. Right, let me show you the timetable.
How many pupils do I have?
Four groups of twenty-five. They’re good kids, but very shy. I’d like you to get them talking a lot. They read and write well, but they speak very little.
I understand. The same thing happened to me with Japanese: I understood everything, but I spoke as if I had stones in my mouth.
Japanese too? How interesting! Right, one more thing: I’d prefer you not to speak Romanian to them in class, even if you’re learning it.
Don’t worry. Even if I wanted to, I couldn’t: I can say “bună ziua”, “mulțumesc” and “zacuscă”.
Ha-ha. With “zacuscă” you can already survive in Romania. Are you nervous?
A little. I feel as if it were my first day at school.
That’s normal. You know what? How good it would be if all new teachers were a little nervous. It means they care.
Thank you. Is there anything I should know about the pupils?
There’s a boy, Andrei, in group C. He’s very bright, but he’s always quiet, as if he didn’t want anyone to see him. I’d like you to try to help him.
I’ll try. I promise that in a month they’ll be speaking as if they’d been living in Spain for years.
Let’s hope so. Come on, I’ll take you there. The children are waiting for you… and believe me, they’re more nervous than you are.
“llevaran años” = had been for years (imperf. subj.)
Run it together: “ko-mo-SEE”. It’s always followed by a little pause and then a verb in -ra: «como si | fuera».
The head teacher uses usted (the formal “you”): siéntase, pase, créame. The verb is in the third person: usted habla, usted es.
OWN-keh: “au” is pronounced like “ow” in “now”, one single syllable.
1. Como si: ALWAYS the imperfect subjunctive
“Como si” (as if, as though) introduces a comparison with something unreal. It is ALWAYS followed by the imperfect subjunctive, even when the sentence is in the present:
She speaks as if she were Spanish. (but she isn’t)
He eats as if he hadn’t eaten for a week.
An exception to the sequence of tenses! “Habla como si FUERA” (not “sea”), even though “habla” is in the present. After como si there is no present subjunctive.
A very common set phrase: como si nada (as if nothing had happened). Se cayó y se levantó como si nada.
In English, the difference is “I hope…” versus “I wish… / If only…”. Ojalá vengas ≈ I hope you come. Ojalá vinieras ≈ I wish you would come / if only you came (I know it’s hard).
3. Polite wishes: me gustaría que, preferiría que
When the main verb is in the CONDITIONAL, the sequence of tenses requires the IMPERFECT subjunctive:
Prefiero que no uses el móvil.
Preferiría que no usaras el móvil.
It’s the most polite way to ask for something in Spanish. Perfect for a boss, a teacher or a client: Me gustaría que me enviara el informe hoy.
a hypothesis / it doesn’t matter: “even if”
Aunque llueva, saldré. (it may rain, it doesn’t matter)
Even if I wanted to, I couldn’t.
Three levels: aunque llueve (I know it’s raining) → aunque llueva (it may rain) → aunque lloviera (it’s unlikely, but even so).
Now you know when the imperfect subjunctive appears:
Habla como si fuera de aquí.
“He speaks as if he were Spanish.”
Ojalá tuviera veinte años otra vez.

I feel as if it were my first day at school.

Ana keeps a diary in Spanish about her new life in Bucharest.
Monday. First lesson. Twenty-five faces looked at me in silence, as if I were an alien. I asked “How are you all?” and nobody answered.
Tuesday. I changed my strategy. I put on Spanish music and asked them to dance. They laughed as if I’d asked them to fly. But three girls danced.
Wednesday. At the bakery, the headscarf lady greeted me as if she’d known me all her life. She gave me a covrig. If only every day started like that.
Thursday. A pupil asked me if people in Spain have a siesta every day. I told him I wish it were true.
Friday. Andrei, the quiet boy from group C, stayed after class. He didn’t say anything. He just left a drawing on my desk: a white cat in a Mexican sombrero.
I wish he could speak the way he draws. Although, come to think of it, maybe he already does speak, in his own way.

Un dibujo de un gato blanco
In the following weeks, Andrei still didn’t speak in class. He sat at the back, by the window, and looked out at the playground as if he were somewhere else.
But every Friday, after the last lesson, he left a drawing on Ana’s desk. He never waited for her to see it. He left it and ran off.
The second drawing was a bull dancing flamenco. The third, the Eiffel Tower in a straw hat. The fourth, a giant paella with legs running through a field of sunflowers.
Ana hung them all on the wall at home. Mihai said it looked like a surrealist art gallery.
“I wish he’d talk,” Ana said to Mihai one evening. “He has so much to say. I can see it in his drawings. But in class he keeps quiet as if he were afraid of making a mistake.”
“What if you don’t ask him to talk?” Mihai answered. “What if you ask him to draw?”
Ana looked at him as if he had just said something brilliant. And maybe he had.
The following Monday, Ana walked into group C with a huge box of felt-tip pens.
“Today we’re not talking,” she announced. “Today we’re making a comic. In Spanish. Each group will invent a story about a cat who travels from Romania to Spain.”
The pupils looked at each other as if they hadn’t understood her. A comic? In Spanish class?
But little by little they started to work. To write the characters’ lines, they had to discuss them in Spanish: “What does the cat say here?”, “No, that’s wrong, you say it like this.”
Without realising it, they were talking. A lot. More than in the whole of the previous month.
Andrei was in a group with two girls and a very chatty boy. At first he didn’t say anything. But when they saw how he drew, his classmates’ jaws dropped.
“Wow! Did you draw that?” one of the girls said, in Spanish, without thinking.
“Then you do the drawings and we’ll write,” suggested the chatty boy. “But you have to tell us what happens in each panel, or we won’t understand.”
And Andrei spoke. Very quietly at first, in short sentences. “Here… the cat gets on the train.” “Here… he’s scared.” “Here… he sees the sea for the first time.”
Ana listened from the other end of the classroom, pretending to mark work. She didn’t dare go closer. She was afraid he would go quiet again if she looked at him.
At the end of the lesson, each group presented its comic. When it was the turn of Andrei’s group, his classmates pushed him forward.
“Let him explain,” they said. “It’s his story.”
Andrei looked at the sheet for a few seconds that felt like hours. Then he looked up and began to speak.
“This is the story of a cat called Tudor. He lives in a village in Romania, but he dreams of seeing the sea. One day he gets on a train without knowing where it’s going…”

He spoke for five minutes. He made a few mistakes, said “el mar” and “la mar”, mixed up the past and the present. But nobody laughed. Everyone listened as if it were the most important story in the world.
When he finished, the whole class applauded. Andrei went back to his seat red-faced, with a smile he couldn’t hide.
That Friday, the drawing on the desk was different. It was Ana, drawn as a superhero with a red and yellow cape, like the Spanish flag.
Underneath, for the first time, there were handwritten words, in almost perfect Spanish:
“Thank you, Miss. I wish all teachers drew.”
Ana had to sit down. She stayed a good while in the empty classroom, with the drawing in her hands, as if she were afraid it would disappear.

That evening, at home, she hung it in the middle of the wall. Mihai looked at it and smiled. “I don’t think you’re in Bucharest as if it were a foreign place any more,” he said. “I think you’re home now.”
Ana stood looking at the drawing for a while longer. She thought about her first day, about the twenty-five silent faces, about how far away everything had seemed back then.
“You’re right,” she told Mihai, resting her head on his shoulder. “Even if I don’t speak Romanian yet, I already feel I belong here. If only Grandma could see this wall.”

Text to read: Mrs Suzuki’s letter
Mrs Suzuki writes to Ana from Madrid.
Dear Ana: the club carries on every Friday, although without you it isn’t the same. Hanako runs it as if she’d been doing it for years.
Tama is fine, but every afternoon she sits on your chair, as if she were waiting for you. If only I could explain to her that you’re far away.
I’d like you to send me photos of your pupils and the drawings you told me about. Kenji says he’d rather you sent him Romanian recipes.
And some news: in April I’m going to Kyoto to see the cherry blossoms with my sister Fumiko. I feel as if I were twenty again. A very big hug, Michiko.
